Self-care teaching in pregnancy 9

What are key points regarding bathing for a pregnant woman?
  • Daily tub baths or showers are ok
  • Hot tubs and saunas are not - maternal core temp is a teratogen in early pregnancy and a fetal-tachycardia risk later.
  • Caution getting in/out of tub. Relaxin loosens ligaments and center of gravity shifts, so fall risk is elevated.
What are key points regarding breast care for a pregnant woman?
  • A firm, supportive bra as breast weight rises.
  • Colostrum may leak in the last months. Wash with clear water only — no soap on the nipples. Soap dries the areola and cracks the skin.
  • Breast shields (pads) may be used to catch leaking colostrum. Do not teach alcohol wipes or "toughening" the nipples.
What are key points regarding clothing for a pregnant woman?
  • Avoid knee-high stockings, garters, and tight clothing. They impede lower-extremity venous return and worsen varicosities and thrombosis risk. Maternity support hose, put on before rising, is the alternative.
  • Wear moderate- or low-heeled shoes. High heels plus a shifted center of gravity are a fall and backache plan.
What are key points regarding sexual activity for a pregnant woman?

Continue as comfort allows.

Three stop rules:

  • ruptured membranes,
  • vaginal bleeding, or
  • risk for preterm labor.

Semen contains prostaglandins and orgasm can stimulate contractions, which is why those three restrictions exist. Shame is not a teaching point. Alternative intimacy is acceptable when intercourse is restricted.

What are key points regarding exercise for a pregnant woman?

Continue exercise.

No contact sports.

Stop and notify the provider for shortness of breath, dizziness, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, or chest pain. Does not require her to quit a sport she already does safely, and it does not cap her at a named heart rate. Contact, collision, and a fall risk are the limits.

What are key points regarding sleep for a pregnant woman?

Left-sided Sims position with pillows: one under the abdomen, one between the legs, one behind the back. -

  • Left side keeps the gravid uterus off the inferior vena cava and improves uterine blood flow.
  • Supine after the first trimester is the position that produces hypotension, dizziness, and decreased placental perfusion.

The pillow set is how you make the left side tolerable for 40 weeks.

What are key points regarding travel for a pregnant woman?
  • No restriction in early pregnancy for uncomplicated clients.
  • Flying is generally acceptable up to 36 weeks. Carry the prenatal record. Airline policy can be stricter; the exam number from this deck is 36 weeks.
  • Car: seat belt with the lap belt low, under the abdomen, and the shoulder belt between the breasts and off the fundus. Airbags stay on.
  • Walk every 2 hours. Avoid long periods of sitting. Pregnancy is hypercoagulable; venous stasis in a car seat is how a deep-vein thrombosis starts.
What are key points regarding work for a pregnant woman?
  • Avoid heavy lifting, long periods of standing, and environmental toxins.
  • Radiation exposure is acceptable if it is monitored and kept below the fetal limit: less than 0.5 rem.

Unmonitored exposure is not "probably fine."

A job next to lead, mercury, solvents, or unmonitored radiation is a teratogen history, not a generic "keep working" answer

What are key points regarding Dental Care for a pregnant woman?

Continue oral hygiene and dental checkups.

Periodontal disease is linked to preterm birth.

Second trimester is the most comfortable window for routine work.

Local anesthetic is acceptable; radiographs with shielding fall under the same monitored-radiation idea as work. Avoid all teratogens.

Teratogens, infections and vaccines 24

Any factor, chemical or physical, that adversely affects the fertilized ovum, embryo, or fetus, is called?

Teratogen

What are the three windows where teratogens can impact a baby?

Preimplantation, weeks 1–2. All or nothing. The conceptus is lost, or it survives without a structural defect. This is why a very early exposure is not automatically “the baby will have a heart defect.”

Embryonic, weeks 3–7 (organogenesis). Major congenital anomalies. This is the window for limb reduction from thalidomide, cardiac and eye defects from rubella, neural-tube defects from folic-acid antagonists, and masculinization from androgens.

Fetal, weeks 8–38. Functional defects and minor anomalies: growth restriction, neurologic injury, tooth staining, ongoing renal effects. Organs are formed; they can still be damaged.

How do Alcohol and cocaine affect a fetus?

Alcohol = Fetal alcohol syndrome - No safe amount. Growth restriction, characteristic facies, neurobehavioral injury.

Cocaine = Abruptio placentae, preterm birth - Vasoconstriction. New bleeding plus recent stimulant use is abruption until proven otherwise.

How do Ace inhibitors and anticonvulsants affect a fetus?

ACE inhibitors = Renal anomalies - Also oligohydramnios and fetal hypotension. Not a pregnancy antihypertensive.

Anticonvulsants = Neural-tube defects, intellectual disability. * Do not stop a needed seizure drug alone; coordinate a safer regimen and folic acid.

A patient taking Warfarin (coumadin) finds out they are pregnant. What alternative medication do they need to be on?

Heparin.

Coumadin (warfarin) = Fetal hemorrhage

  • Crosses the placenta. Heparin does not, which is why anticoagulation plans change.
How can cytomegalovirus affect a fetus?

Cytomegalovirus = Microcephaly, blindness, intellectual disability

  • Body fluids of young children. Hand hygiene after diapers; do not share cups.
How can folic acid antagonists affect a fetus?

Folic Acid deficiency = Neural-tube defects

  • Methotrexate-class drugs. Why preconception folic acid exists.
How do lead, lithium, and mercury affect a fetus?

Lead = Central nervous system damage

  • Old paint, some imported pottery and cosmetics, battery plants.

Lithium = Ebstein anomaly

  • Cardiac defect (apical displacement of the tricuspid valve). Needs a specialist plan, not abrupt stopping.

Mercury = Neurologic damage

  • High-mercury fish. "foods to limit" list
How can rubella, varicella and syphilis affect a fetus?

Rubella = Deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects

  • Worst in the first trimester. Live vaccine waits until after birth.

Syphilis = Congenital syphilis

  • Treat with penicillin. Desensitize if allergic. Do not substitute.

Varicella = Limb and eye defects

  • Congenital varicella syndrome if early. Live vaccine is postpartum only.
How can Vitamin A and its derivatives affect a fetus?

Vitamin A and derivatives = Spontaneous abortion, cardiac and facial defects

  • Isotretinoin and high-dose retinol. Prenatal vitamins use a safe amount.
What are the TORCH teratogens?

T = Toxoplasmosis - from undercooked meat, cat litter, and garden soil.

O = Other: syphilis, varicella, parvovirus, hep B, HIV, and Zika.

R = Rubella

C = Cytomegalovirus

H = Herpes Simplex

How is Toxoplasmosis acquired and what teaching should you provide to a pregnant client?

Toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasma gondii from undercooked meat, cat litter, and garden soil.

Congenital picture: intracranial calcifications, hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis.

Teaching: someone else changes the box, cook meat through, wash produce, gloves for gardening.

How is Herpes simplex acquired and what teaching should you provide to a pregnant client?

Usually acquired during vaginal birth through an active lesion. Primary infection in pregnancy is worse than a recurrence.

Suppression from 36 weeks. Active genital lesions or prodrome in labor: cesarean.

Which vaccines are contraindicated for pregnancy?

Live Vax: MMR, varicella, and live-attenuated intranasal influenza are contraindicated.

Give inactivated influenza any trimester and tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) at 27–36 weeks.

MMR and varicella go postpartum, including if the client is breastfeeding.

Avoid conception for about 1 month after a live vaccine.

How do tobacco and nicotine affect a fetus?

Vasoconstriction and carbon monoxide. Growth restriction, previa and abruption risk, preterm birth. Cessation is the goal.

Nicotine replacement is not the first teaching line on most nursing exams.

How is HIV managed with a pregnant client?

Screen at the first visit and again in the third trimester when risk is high.

  • Antiretroviral therapy through pregnancy drives the viral load down and cuts perinatal transmission sharply.
  • If the load is 1,000 copies/mL or higher, or unknown, near term, plan a cesarean at about 38 weeks and intravenous zidovudine in labor.
  • Avoid a fetal scalp electrode, forceps, vacuum, and episiotomy when possible.
  • Start neonatal zidovudine promptly. Diagnose the infant with a virologic test, not an antibody test — maternal immunoglobulin G crosses the placenta and makes an uninfected infant antibody-positive for months.

DO NOT BREASTFEED if formula is available.

How is Group B Strep (GBS) handled with a pregnant client?

Not a sexually transmitted infection. It lives in the gastrointestinal and genital tract and causes early-onset neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis.

Screen with a vaginorectal swab at 36-38 weeks (older items say 35-37).

If a pregnant client is + for GBS, what steps are taken?

Give intravenous penicillin G in labor for a positive screen, GBS bacteriuria at any time during pregnancy, a prior infant with invasive GBS disease, or unknown status plus preterm labor, rupture of membranes of 18 hours or more, or intrapartum fever.

A planned cesarean with intact membranes and no labor does not need prophylaxis for a positive screen alone.

  • An oral course in the office does not clear colonization.
How is Chlamydia handled with a pregnant client?
  • Often silent
  • Azithromycin 1 g once
  • Possible Effect: Neonatal conjunctivitis and later afebrile pneumonia; preterm birth
How is Gonorrhea handled with a pregnant client?
  • Often silent; yellow-green discharge
  • Ceftriaxone intramuscular
  • Effect: Severe ophthalmia. Erythromycin ointment at birth is prophylaxis, not a substitute for treating the parent.

Gonorrhea can cause premature rupture of membranes.

How is Syphilis handled with a pregnant client?

Chancre, then rash including palms and soles

Benzathine penicillin G; desensitize if allergic

Congenital syphilis is preventable. Do not substitute another drug.

How are Trichomoniasis and Bacterial vaginosis handled with a pregnant client?

Trichomoniasis: Frothy green-yellow, odor

TX: Metronidazole; no alcohol

Effect: Preterm birth. Treat the partner.

Bacterial vaginosis: Thin gray discharge, fishy odor, clue cells

TX: Metronidazole

Effect: Preterm birth and postpartum endometritis

How is Candidiasis handled with a pregnant client?

Candidiasis: Thick white, itch, no fishy odor

TX: Topical azole for 7 days

Effect: Comfort problem more than a congenital infection

How is Hep B handled with a pregnant client?

Hepatitis B: Often silent,

TX: Identify surface antigen

TX: Neonate gets immune globulin and vaccine within 12 hours, at separate sites

Nutrition, discomforts and danger signs 19

What are standard weight gain metrics for pregnancy?

Average woman: 25 to 35 lb.

BMI under 18.5 (underweight): 28 to 40 lb.

BMI over 25 (overweight): 15 to 25 lb.

BMI over 30 (obese): 11 to 20 lb.

Pattern matters. Most of the gain is second and third trimester, about 2 to 4 lb in the first.

A normal-BMI client who has gained 6 lb at 32 weeks is undergaining.

A client who has gained 20 lb by week 16 is not “ahead of schedule.”

Where weight goes, so “I only need to eat for 7 pounds of baby” fails: fetus about 7 to 8 lb, placenta 1 to 2, amniotic fluid about 2, uterus about 2, breasts about 2, increased blood volume 3 to 4, extracellular fluid 3 to 4, maternal stores several pounds.

What are the caloric and intake considerations for pregnancy?

Calories. no extra in the first trimester if the baseline diet was adequate; about 340 extra kcal/day in the second trimester and 452 extra in the third.

  • Lactation adds 450 to 500 kcal/day.

Protein. About 71 g/day, up from about 46 g. Growth of fetal tissue and expanded maternal blood volume. Adolescents and twins sit at the high end.

Fat. Needed for fetal brain and for calorie density. Emphasize oils rather than solid fats. Omega-3 sources from low-mercury fish support retina and brain.

What are the vitamin and mineral considerations for pregnancy?
  • Vitamins. A prenatal vitamin covers gaps. Excess vitamin A (retinol, isotretinoin) is a teratogen — cardiac and facial defects, spontaneous abortion. Beta-carotene from food is not the same problem.
  • Minerals the slide names. Calcium and phosphorus for fetal bone; the fetus will take calcium from maternal bone if intake is low.
  • Folic acid for neural-tube closure (400 mcg before conception, 600 mcg in pregnancy, 4 mg if a prior neural-tube defect).
  • Iodine for fetal thyroid and brain (about 220 mcg).
  • Iron for expanded red-cell mass (27 mg; take with vitamin C, not with milk, tea, or coffee).
  • Sodium is not severely restricted in a healthy pregnancy; severe salt restriction is an old idea that fails.

Zinc supports growth; high-dose iron can compete with it.

What are the fluid and fiber considerations for pregnancy?
  • Fluid. About 8 to 10 glasses (2.3 L) a day. Dehydration triggers contractions.
  • Fiber. Constipation is expected from progesterone and from iron. Fluid, fiber, and walking before a stimulant laxative.
What should you educate a pregnant client on regarding food safety?
  • Heat deli meat and hot dogs until steaming;
  • Skip unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses unless the label says pasteurized;
  • Skip refrigerated smoked seafood unless cooked;

cook meat and eggs through;

  • Avoid shark, swordfish, king mackerel, and tilefish; limit albacore tuna; (high mercury!)
  • Caffeine 200 mg/day or less (the limit your course quiz uses)

✅ Your NUR 234 quiz uses 200 mg a day; the set said 200 to 300.

Cravings for nonfood substances in pregnancy is called.....

Pica: An indication for referral to the primary care provider for iron-deficiency anemia evaluation.

Ice, clay, dirt, starch, and freezer frost are the usual substances.

  • Clay and dirt can also bind minerals and carry pathogens.
  • Name the substance, estimate how much, check hemoglobin, and do not call it a personality quirk.
What are some nursing interventions to support a pregnant client with pyrosis?

Pyrosis is heartburn from progesterone relaxing the lower esophageal sphincter plus the growing uterus compressing the stomach.

  • Small, frequent meals.
  • Sleep on the left side with two pillows.
  • Wait 2 hours after eating before lying down.
  • Avoid fatty and spicy foods, caffeine, chocolate, carbonated drinks, and acidic foods such as tomato products and orange juice.
  • Wear loose clothing.
  • Do not smoke. Smoking worsens reflux and is already a teratogen exposure.

A provider-approved antacid can be added if those measures fail

When does pyrosis become concerning?

The danger-sign version is epigastric or right-upper-quadrant pain plus headache or visual change — that is preeclampsia, not pyrosis.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant adolescent?

Still growing her own skeleton while feeding a fetus. Irregular meals, body image, food insecurity.

Upper end of the BMI gain range.

Calcium 1,300 mg if under 19.

Concrete food swaps, not a lecture about vanity.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant woman >40yo?

Decreased nutritional stores. More preexisting hypertension, diabetes, and thyroid disease.

Diet history plus a look at chronic-disease medicines that may be teratogenic (ACE inhibitors). Do not assume stores are full.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant woman with decreased nutritional stores (malnutrition, illness)?

Close spacing, lactation, poverty, or a prior restrictive diet.

Rebuild before and during pregnancy.

  • Folic acid and iron are the first gaps.
What are some unique considerations for a pregnant overweight woman (BMI>25)?

Gain 15-25 lb, not 25-35. Higher risk of gestational diabetes, macrosomia, and hypertension.

Quality of intake, not a weight-loss diet. Forbid weight-loss diets.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant underweight woman (BMI<18.5)?

Gain target 28-40 lb. Higher risk of a low-birth-weight infant.

Do not praise a small gain. Add calorie-dense, nutrient-dense foods.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant obese woman (BMI>30)?

Gain 11-20 lb.

Same rule: do not prescribe a deficit. Screen earlier for glucose intolerance.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant woman who had bariatric surgery?

Small pouch, risk of dumping with sugar loads, and deficits of iron, vitamin B12, folate, and calcium.

Small frequent meals, protein first, a bariatric-level supplement, not a standard prenatal alone. Avoid simple sugars if dumping occurs.

What are some unique considerations for a pregnant woman who is a vegetarian?

Can be adequate if planned. Strict vegan diets miss vitamin B12.

Complementary proteins across the day. Reliable B12. Watch iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, and DHA.

Severe nausea and vomiting with inability to maintain usual nutrition during pregnancy is called?

Hyperemesis gravidarum

Morning nausea is dry crackers, small meals, and a call if it worsens.

Hyperemesis is weight loss, ketonuria, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance.

What nursing interventions and teaching are used for hyperemesis gravidarum?

Nothing by mouth briefly if vomiting is continuous; IV fluid with correction of electrolytes and often thiamine before glucose in a depleted client;

antiemetics the provider orders (vitamin B6, doxylamine, and others);

advance from clear liquids to small, frequent, low-fat meals as tolerated;

emotional support, because this is miserable and isolating.

Rule out other causes (thyroid, gastrointestinal, multiple gestation, molar pregnancy) rather than calling every vomiting client hyperemesis. Unchecked vomiting treated only with ginger for weeks is how a client ends up in ketosis.

What are key danger signs that override other normal pregnancy education?
  • Vaginal bleeding — also a stop rule for sex and a reason to stop exercise.
  • Leaking fluid — stop sex, stop tub baths, come in.
  • Regular contractions before 37 weeks that do not stop with rest and fluids.
  • Severe headache, visual change, epigastric or right-upper-quadrant pain. Not pyrosis teaching.
  • Decreased fetal movement once movement has been established.
  • Dysuria with fever or flank pain.
  • Sudden face and hand swelling, or a hot swollen calf.
  • Persistent vomiting with inability to keep fluids down — hyperemesis pathway, not crackers.

M6Labor & Birth 112 cards

Open the Module 6 page

Signs that labor is near 5

Sinking of the fetal head into the true pelvis is what preliminary sign of labor?

Lightening

What to expect: Easier breathing, more pelvic pressure and urinary frequency. Happens days to weeks before labor in a primip, often later in a multip.

What state is the cervix in just prior to labor initiating?

Ripening of the cervix: Prostaglandins soften the cervix for shortening and dilatation

  • A soft cervix is preparation, not an emergency.
How should a client respond when their membrane ruptures?

Membranes have ruptured with release of amniotic fluid = Come in. Note time, color, and odor. This is also a stop rule for intercourse and tub baths.

What is it called when the Internal cervical mucus plug has been released?

Show

Blood-tinged mucus. Different from bleeding like a period, which is a danger sign.

What is the true beginning of labor?

Uterine Contractions

Regular, stronger, longer, not stopped by rest. Braxton Hicks are the irregular ones that fade.

The 5 Ps: passage and passenger 54

What are the key concepts related to the 5 descriptions of fetal location (lie, presentation, attitude, position and station)?
  • LIE = Which direction is the fetus lying?
  • PRESENTATION = What body part is coming first? (Vertex)
  • ATTITUDE = How is the fetal head/body flexed or extended?
  • POSITION = Which way is the presenting landmark pointing inside the maternal pelvis? (LOA/ROA)
  • STATION = How far down has the presenting part descended? (0 Station)
  • Vertex" answers PRESENTATION (a flexed, head-first presentation). "LOA" answers POSITION. "0 station" answers DESCENT/ENGAGEMENT.
What are the 5 P's of labor?

passage - The maternal route: pelvis + cervix + vagina + pelvic floor/perineum.

passenger- The fetus: size, skull, lie, presentation, attitude, position, engagement, station.

Position - The laboring person's body position.

powers - Uterine contractions + maternal pushing.

Psyche - Fear, coping, confidence, support, stress response.

What can go wrong with each of the 5 P's?

Passage - Small/poorly fitting pelvic dimensions, cervical resistance, full bladder.

passenger- Malpresentation, poor flexion, large presenting diameter, failure to descend.

Position - Supine can reduce venous return and uteroplacental perfusion; upright/side-lying/hands-and-knees may help.

Powers - Weak contractions, tachysystole, ineffective pushing, inadequate rest between contractions.

Psyche - Fear/stress can increase catecholamines and interfere with labor progress.

What does labor passage entail and how can it impact whether labor is abnormal?

Passage is the route from the uterus to the external perineum. It is the bony pelvis plus the soft tissues: cervix, vagina, pelvic floor muscles, and perineum.

Think inlet, the midpelvis, and the outlet.

  • The fetal head has to clear the narrowest diameter at each level.
  • The inlet is the pelvic brim. A head that cannot enter the inlet never engages.
  • The midpelvis is often the narrowest plane. Ischial spines mark station zero and are the landmark for engagement.
  • The outlet is the bony exit. A tight outlet is felt as prolonged crowning and a higher laceration risk.
  • Soft-tissue resistance falls as the cervix effaces and dilates and as the pelvic floor stretches. A full bladder is soft-tissue obstruction. Empty it.
What can cause passage issues?

Calling every slow labor "she is not trying" ignores passage. A contracted pelvis or a full bladder will not yield to more coaching. The fix is position change, bladder emptying, and a provider evaluation for cephalopelvic disproportion, not louder pushing.

What are key aspects of the passenger that can impact labor?

Considerations - The structure of the fetal skull, diameters of the fetal skull, molding, and fetal presentation and position.

What are the components/factors related to the passenger?

(Lie, presentation, Attitude, position, and Station)

LIE → direction of the whole fetus.

PRESENTATION → first body part at the cervix.

ATTITUDE → fetal flexion/extension.

POSITION → direction the landmark points in the maternal pelvis.

STATION → vertical level relative to the ischial spines.

What is molding?

The fetal skull is not one bone. Sutures and fontanels let the bones overlap, which is molding.

  • Molding is expected and resolves in a day or two. It is not the same as caput succedaneum, the soft scalp edema from pressure, or a cephalohematoma, bleeding under the periosteum that does not cross suture lines.
  • A molded head can look larger than the true biparietal diameter, so do not use the swollen scalp to decide that the head is too big.
What is attitude and what are the 4 head attitudes for a fetus?

Attitude is the relation of fetal parts to each other.

  • The normal attitude is general flexion: chin on chest, arms folded, legs flexed.
  • Vertex, full flexion. Smallest diameter. This is the expected vaginal-birth attitude.
  • Military, moderate flexion. Head is neither flexed nor extended. Larger diameter, slower descent.
  • Brow, partial extension. Largest diameter. Often will not deliver vaginally unless it converts.
  • Face, complete extension. The face is the presenting part. A mentum-anterior face may deliver vaginally. A mentum-posterior face cannot extend further under the symphysis and is a cesarean indication if it does not rotate.
What is the expected vaginal-birth attitude?

Vertex, full flexion. Smallest diameter.

Which attitude has a slower descent, and why?

Military, moderate flexion.

  • Head is neither flexed nor extended. Larger diameter, slower descent.
Which attitudes will not likely deliver vaginally?
  • Brow, partial extension. Largest diameter. Often will not deliver vaginally unless it converts.
  • Face, complete extension. The face is the presenting part. A mentum-posterior face cannot extend further under the symphysis and is a cesarean indication if it does not rotate.
  • A mentum-anterior face may deliver vaginally.
What are the types of fetal lie?

Fetal lie = direction of the fetal spine/body

Think of fetal lie as asking: “Is the baby’s body pointing the same direction as Mom’s body?”

Longitudinal lie = baby is vertical. Mom’s spine runs roughly up and down. If the baby’s spine also runs up and down, the baby is in a longitudinal lie.

  • But that does not tell us which end of the baby is down. Could be head down (cephalic) or butt down (breech)

Transverse lie is perpendicular (mom up/down, baby side-to-side). Presents as a shoulder.

Oblique lie is at an angle and usually converts to longitudinal or transverse.

What is the key distinction b/w lie and presentation?

LIE = direction of the baby's whole body.

PRESENTATION = which part is coming out first.

Longitudinal + head down = cephalic

Longitudinal + butt/feet down = breech

Transverse = sideways → shoulder presentation

If the baby is cephalic, how is the head positioned?

“Exactly WHICH part of the head is entering the pelvis first?”

Vertex = head flexed, chin tucked to chest, back/top of head presents first = BEST for vag birth

Brow = head partially extended, chin lifting, forehead presents first = DIFFICULT

Face = head fully extended, Head tipped way backward, face presents first - IFFY position

Chin DOWN → Vertex

Chin coming UP → Brow

Chin WAY UP → Face

What fetal positions are common with a baby in vertex?

Vertex = chin tucked - Picture the baby looking down at its own chest.

This is the position you want.

  • The baby's neck is flexed, so the occiput (back of the head) becomes the important landmark.

This is why you see fetal positions such as:

L/ROA = Left/Right Occiput Anterior

LOP = Left Occiput Posterior

The O is there because this is a vertex presentation, so we use the occiput to describe position.

Why is vertex a favorable birthing position?

Because flexing the head allows a smaller diameter of the skull to enter the pelvis.

Why does a brow presentation create a difficult birth?

Brow = chin starting to lift - baby starts looking forward/upward instead of keeping the chin tucked.

Now the forehead/brow is trying to enter the pelvis.

The problem is that this presents a very large diameter of the fetal head.

Brow = partially extended head → poor fit through pelvis.

It often needs to convert into another presentation for vaginal delivery to occur.

Why does the face position use the Mentum for landmarking?

Face = head completely extended - Imagine the baby throwing its head all the way backward, almost looking behind itself.

Now the face is presenting. And something important changes:

We can't use the occiput as our position landmark anymore. Instead, we use the baby's chin, called the mentum.

Vertex → landmark = Occiput (O)

Face → landmark = Mentum (M)

What is the story for this patient: Longitudinal lie → cephalic presentation → vertex → LOA → station −2

Longitudinal lie = Baby is lying vertically.

↓

Cephalic = Baby is head down.

↓

Vertex = Baby's chin is tucked, so the back/top of the head comes first.

↓

LOA = The occiput points toward Mom's left-front.

↓

−2 station = The head is still 2 cm above the ischial spines and therefore isn't engaged yet.

In what order do you describe where the fetus is?

LIE: Which direction is the baby lying?

↓

PRESENTATION: What body part is coming first?

↓

ATTITUDE: If it's the head, how flexed/extended is it?

↓

POSITION: Which direction is the presenting landmark pointing?

↓

STATION: How far down is it?

What are head position considerations?
  • TUCK → VERTEX → OCCIPUT → GOOD FIT
  • PARTIAL EXTENSION → BROW → FOREHEAD → BAD FIT
  • FULL EXTENSION → FACE → MENTUM/CHIN → MAY OR MAY NOT DELIVER VAGINALLY
What is a presentation and what are the three types?

Presentation is the part that enters the pelvic inlet first. The deck lists three: cephalic, breech, and shoulder.

  • Cephalic is head first.
  • Breech is buttocks or feet first.
  • Shoulder is a transverse lie.
What is the most common and least concerning presentation?

Cephalic is head first.

Vertex (chin tucked) is the well-flexed subset and is the expected presentation.

Face and brow are cephalic but poorly flexed, so not great for vaginal delivery.

What are complete, frank, footling breech positions?
  • Breech is buttocks or feet first.
  • Complete breech has flexed hips and knees.
  • Frank breech has flexed hips and extended knees, feet by the head.
  • Footling breech has one or both feet presenting. -
Which position risks cord prolapse?

Breech raises cord-prolapse risk because the buttocks do not seal the cervix the way a head does, and it raises head-entrapment risk because the body can deliver before the head has molded.

Which presentation requires a cesarean section?
  • Shoulder is a transverse lie. A cesarean is required. Do not attempt vaginal birth. An arm prolapsing through the cervix is a presenting part that cannot deliver and a cord-compression emergency.
________ is which part is coming first: head (cephalic), buttocks (breech), or shoulder.

Presentation

______ is the fetal spine compared with the mother's spine: longitudinal or transverse.

Lie

________ is flexion versus extension of the fetal head. ________ is how far down that part is, relative to the ischial spines.

Attitude

Station - Station is only descent. It answers how far the presenting part has moved through the pelvis, in centimeters, using the ischial spines as zero. It does not say which part is coming first, which way that part faces, or how open the cervix is.

What is the landmark for Station and the measurement indicators?

The landmark is the pair of ischial spines, the narrow bony points on either side of the midpelvis. On a vaginal exam the examiner finds the lowest part of the presenting part and estimates how many centimeters it sits above or below those spines.

  • Negative is still high. The presenting part is above the spines. Station −2 means about 2 cm above the spines. NOT ENGAGED
  • Zero is engaged. The presenting part is at the spines.
  • Positive is moving out. Descending toward outlet; larger positive number = closer to birth.

Deck scale, −5 to +5

What is the risk if the membrane ruptures while station is still high (-2)?

If membranes rupture while the presenting part is HIGH/UNENGAGED (negative station), the umbilical cord has room to slip below it → cord prolapse risk. After ROM, assess fetal heart rate first.

________ is the direction the presenting landmark points: left or right, and front, side, or back.

Position

Three letter designation

  • 1st letter- maternal pelvic side (Left/Right, L/R)
  • 2nd - Presenting landmark (Occiput, Mentum (face), Sacrum (breech)
  • 3rd - Direction landmark faces (Anterior/Posterior/Transverse)
What is included in this statement "vertex, left occiput anterior, station 0"?

presentation, position, and station.

How do you read the three letters of a fetal position?

Read left to right. Each letter answers one question.

First letter: which side of the mother. R is the mother’s right. L is the mother’s left. This is her pelvis, not yours as you face her.

Middle letter: the landmark on the presenting part. This is the denominator. It changes with presentation.

O is occiput, the back of the fetal head. Used for a vertex, the well-flexed head-first presentation.

M is mentum, the chin. Used for a face presentation.

S is sacrum. Used for a breech.

Sc or A is scapula or acromion. Used for a shoulder. A transverse lie cannot deliver vaginally, so this label is a cesarean finding, not a pushing plan.

Last letter: front, back, or side of the mother. A is anterior, toward the pubic symphysis and the mother’s abdomen. P is posterior, toward the sacrum and her back. T is transverse, straight to the side, neither front nor back.

What does Left Occiput Anterior mean for the baby's positioning?

LEFT OCCIPUT ANTERIOR: the fetus is vertex/head-first, and the back of the fetal head (occiput) points toward the mother's LEFT FRONT.

  • The fetal back is against the mother's left-front abdominal wall.
  • That is where the heart is heard best, in the left lower quadrant.

Most favorable position - ROA is also favorable

Which position typically rotates?

LOT - Occiput is on mothers Left, fetal back is left side, transitional - usually rotates

ROT - Occiput is on mothers right, fetal back is right side, transitional - usually rotates

Transverse (LOT, ROT) is a waypoint. Most of these rotate to anterior during descent. A question that says "arrest of rotation in occiput transverse" is a powers or passage problem, not a normal LOT finding.

Why is anterior more favorable?

Anterior (back of head towards the belly/abdomen) is favorable because the head is already facing the right way for birth.

In which position is the head born with the occiput coming under the pubic symphysis?

Occiput anterior (LOA or ROA), a vertex presentation. The head is born by extension, with the occiput coming under the pubic symphysis.

✅ The set answered "vertex"; the position that matters here is occiput anterior.

Which position is "sunny side up" and what are the concerns with it?

Posterior is "sunny side up." The face is toward the mother's abdomen and the hard occiput is pressed into her sacrum. That pressure is the back labor: constant sacral pain, worse in the contraction, not relieved by the usual belly-breathing cues.

  • The head must rotate much farther, often 135 degrees, to become anterior. Until it does, descent is slow, the second stage is longer, and vacuum or forceps are more likely. Hands-and-knees and sacral counterpressure are the nursing moves. Persistent occiput posterior is not an automatic cesarean.
Describe the baby's position: "Longitudinal lie, vertex presentation, flexed attitude, LOA position, station 0."

Translation: fetus is lined up vertically; head comes first; chin is tucked; occiput points to mother's left-front; head is engaged at the ischial spines.

Describe the baby's position- "Longitudinal lie, vertex presentation, ROP position, station -2."

Translation: head first, but occiput points toward mother's right-back; head is still 2 cm above the ischial spines and is NOT engaged.

  • Expect possible back labor and slower rotation.
What is the key difference between vertex and LOA?

Vertex ≠ LOA.

Vertex tells WHAT is presenting and that the head is flexed.

LOA tells WHICH DIRECTION the occiput points. The O already tells you the head is first: the occiput is only used as the landmark for a vertex.

  • Station tells HOW LOW it is.

✅ Corrected: the set said LOA does not show which end is down. The O (occiput) means the head is first.

What are the four maneuvers to manipulate/map the baby's location?

Leopold maneuvers

  • Fundal grip
  • Umbilical/lateral grip
  • Pawlik grip
  • Pelvic grip

You are trying to answer:

What is at the top? → Where is the back? → What is at the bottom? → Is the head flexed and descending?

What do fetal body parts feel like externally?

Hard + round + smooth = HEAD

Soft + broad + irregular = BUTTOCKS

Smooth + firm + long surface = BACK

Small + knobby + moving parts = ARMS/LEGS

What findings are important when doing a fundal grip?

Fundus/top of uterus. Question you're answering:

“What fetal part is up here?”

Head UP → breech

Butt UP → head down/cephalic

What findings are important when doing an umbilical/lateral grip?

Feel the SIDES - Now put your hands on the sides of the uterus.

You're trying to find: “Which side is the baby's BACK on?”

One side should feel relatively: smooth + firm + continuous = That's the baby's back.

The opposite side feels: knobby + irregular + little moving parts = Those are the arms and legs.

Why do I care where the back is and why do I perform an umbilical/lateral grip

Because that's generally where you want to place the external fetal heart rate transducer.

What findings are important when doing pawlik grip?

Feel just above the pubic bone

Now you're at the bottom of the uterus, just above the pubic symphysis.

You're asking:

“What part is actually PRESENTING at the pelvis?”

If you feel something: hard + round = HEAD

Can I move it?

If the head is easily movable or “ballotable,” it hasn't settled firmly into the pelvis.

Think: Movable head → NOT engaged yet.

#3 = What's DOWN, and is it ENGAGED?

If the head is movable during a Pawlik grip exam, what does this indicate?

If the head is easily movable or “ballotable,” it hasn't settled firmly into the pelvis.

Think: Movable head → NOT engaged yet.

If it's firmly down in the pelvis and difficult to move, it is more likely engaged.

What findings are important when doing pelvic grip?

Leopold #4 — Face Mom's feet and feel down toward the pelvis

You're essentially getting more information about the head: “How is the head entering the pelvis?”

You're helping confirm descent and fetal head attitude—especially whether the head is flexed.

What four questions do the four Leopold maneuvers answer?

1 — What's UP? (Head or butt)

2 — Where's the BACK? (Left or right)

3 — What's DOWN? Is it ENGAGED? (can you move it)

4 — How's the HEAD entering the pelvis?

To answer, check:

TOP → SIDE → BOTTOM → PELVIS

What two things does the nurse do before performing Leopold maneuvers?

Have the patient empty her bladder and perform the palpation between contractions, because a full bladder or contraction can interfere with the assessment.

What's the difference in findings between a Leopold maneuver set and a vaginal exam?
  • Leopold maneuvers are how you estimate lie, presentation, position, and attitude from the outside.
  • A vaginal exam is what gives you the more precise information about cervical dilation, effacement, and station.

Movements, stages and ruptured membranes 30

What is the order of the movements of labor?
  • Engagement: widest transverse head diameter passes the pelvic inlet; clinically station 0.
  • Descent: head moves downward through the pelvis.
  • Flexion: chin tucks more firmly, presenting a smaller head diameter.
  • Internal rotation: occiput rotates, usually toward anterior, to fit the pelvic outlet.
  • Extension: head extends under the pubic symphysis and is born.
  • External rotation/restitution: head turns back to line up with the shoulders.
  • Expulsion: shoulders and body are born.
What is the difference b/w extension and external rotation?

Movement that delivers the HEAD = extension.

Movement after the head is born as it realigns with the shoulders = external rotation/restitution.

What does dilation measure?

Dilation measures the opening of the cervix

Range: 0-10cm

Tells us: How OPEN is the cervix?

What does Effacement measure?

Thinning/shortening of cervix

Range: 0-100%

Tells us: How THIN is the cervix?

What does Station measure?

Descent relative to ischial spines

Range: negative - 0 - positive

How LOW is the presenting part?

A 38wk pregnant patient is having contractions and the following readings- "6 cm / 80% / -1"

What does this mean?

= cervix is 6 cm open, 80% thinned, and presenting part is still 1 cm above the ischial spines.

How do you count frequency and duration of a contraction?
  • Frequency = beginning of one contraction to beginning of the next.
  • Duration = time of beginning to end of the SAME contraction.
How does the peak, increment, and decrement relate to contractions?

Increment = contraction builds; acme = peak; decrement = contraction falls.

How do you measure the intensity of a contraction?

Intensity = strength at the peak (acme).

  • External monitoring does not directly measure mm Hg intensity; an intrauterine pressure catheter does.
Why does relaxation between contractions matter?

Relaxation matters because uteroplacental blood flow recovers between contractions.

What are the three parts of the 1st stage of labor?

1st Stage: early/latent - Onset regular contractions → before active; example 2 cm/50%.

  • Contractions are mild 20-40sec
  • Client is talkative, anxious, can usually cope

1st stage - active: Begins around 6cm; 40-60sec, about q3-5min

  • Client is more focused/inward, needs more coping support

1st stage- transition: About 8-10cm and 100%; 60-70sec, about q2-3min.

  • Client is shaking, nausea, irritability, I can't do this, urge to push
What occurs during the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th stages of labor?

2nd - 10cm/100% = birth - crowning

3rd - Birth and placental delivery- gush, cord lengthens, uterus rises/firm/globular

4th - first 1-4hr after placenta, recovery, major hemorrhage= surveillance period.

What is it called when the membrane ruptures on its own?

Spontaneous rupture of membranes (SROM)

What is it called when the membrane ruptures >1 hour before labor begins?

Premature ROM (PROM) - can occur at term; premature here means before labor (not related to weeks of gestation)

PPROM = Preterm premature ROM before end of 36th week = adds risk.

What is artificial ROM/Amniotomy?

AROM = Provider manually ruptures membranes.

What does green or brown amniotic fluid indicate?

Meconium, fecal stool in the fluid - can be a sign of a problem.

Post-term - mature gut or hypoxia.

Contact neonatal team for birth.

What does a 10cm cervical dilation look like size-wise?

A bagel!

1cm = cheerio

5 cm = round slice of lime

What is the priority sequence after ROM?
  • Assess Fetal Heart Rate FIRST → 2) confirm ROM (nitrazine/pooling; fern testing may also be used) → 3) document COLOR, ODOR, AMOUNT, TIME → 4) monitor for infection/prolapse.
What are the 4 findings post-ROM that a nurse should assess?

Clear or pale/light yellow → expected amniotic fluid

Green/brown → think meconium (fetal stool)

Foul-smelling → think infection - Foul odor + maternal fever/fetal tachycardia/uterine tenderness = infection concern.

Bloody/dark red → concerning for bleeding, not normal amniotic fluid

“Patient reports a sudden gush of fluid. What should the nurse do FIRST?”

Assess fetal heart rate

What type of contractions are expected during the latent phase of labor?

Contractions every 5-30 minutes, shorter duration (:30 to 1 minute).

0-30% effaced cervix

What hormone stimulates uterine contractions?

Oxytocin

Pitocin is synthetic oxytocin, given to induce or augment labor.

✅ The set said "cervical contractions"; oxytocin contracts the uterus.

What is key to monitor during the latent phase of labor, and why?

Fetal heart rate - to determine if the fetus is receiving an adequate amount of oxygen. Use fetal monitor.

At what stage of labor should the mom go to the hospital?

Active phase: from about 6 cm (your course slides and ATI; older sources say 4 cm) until full dilation at 10 cm

Contractions are stronger and longer

Water may break (amniotic sac ruptures)

Pain management (non-RX, epidural, IV narcotics (slowly during peak of contraction)

✅ Your course slides start the active phase at about 6 cm; the set said 4 cm.

What does a station of -3 mean?

3cm above the ischial spine (higher up in the abdomen, further from the exit)

  • numbers are above the spines

+ numbers are below (closer to exit). A higher + number means baby birth is coming.

What are key differences b/w True and False Labor?

False labor is:

  • Irregular
  • No change to intensity over time
  • Abdominal pain only
  • No cervical changes (dilation, effacement)
  • Walking/rest helps pain

True Labor:

  • Regular intervals
  • Intensity increases
  • Back to front pain
  • Cervical changes
  • Walking makes it worse.
How can nitrazine paper confirm rupture of membranes?

Nitrazine tape confirms the rupture of membranes (ROM) by measuring the pH of vaginal secretions. Because amniotic fluid is significantly more alkaline than normal vaginal environment, contact with it alters the color of the indicator strip.

Normal Vaginal pH: Typically acidic, ranging between 4.5 and 6.0.

Amniotic Fluid pH: Structurally basic/alkaline, ranging between 7.1 and 7.3

What does a nurse want to document in terms of amniotic fluid? COAT

COAT

Color

Odor

Amount

Time - prolonged ROM can lead to maternal infection

What occurs during the third stage of labor?

1- placental separation- Placenta pulls away from uterus.

  • Occurs within 30 minutes of delivery. Longer could be a sign of an issue. Uterus can't contract down, which can cause hemorrhage. Provider will remove manually or through a D&C (scrape the walls), if not, she may need surgery.
  • Cord lengthens as it comes out. DO NOT TUG ON CORD.
  • Gush of blood when it comes out.

2- Placental Expulsion - comes out.

When does the recovery stage (4th stage) happen?

1-4 hours after delivery of the placenta

What are the three things you measure during labor?

Progress of labor: Dilation, effacement, station

Contractions: frequency, duration, intensity

FHR: baseline HR, variability, periodic changes (stress test)

  • Decelerations are the focus (early, late, variable)

Bishop score and oxytocin 13

What does a Bishop score indicate?

“If we induce labor, how ready is this cervix to actually deliver a baby?”

A higher Bishop score = cervix is more favorable (“ripe”) for induction. ≥8 as favorable.

OPEN + THIN + SOFT + FORWARD + BABY LOW = favorable for induction.

What are the 5 components of a Bishop Score?

Dilation - How open is the cervix? Better = More dilated

Effacement - How thin/short is the cervix?= More effaced

Station- How far has the fetal head descended? + score/lower head

Consistency- How firm or soft is the cervix? Soft

Position: Where is the cervix pointing? Anterior

How does cervix position change before and during birth?

Before labor, the cervix tends to sit more posteriorly, toward the mother's back.

As the cervix ripens and prepares for labor, it generally moves more anteriorly, toward the front.

Think:

Posterior → midposition → anterior

For Bishop:

ANTERIOR = more favorable.

Important: don't confuse this with fetal position

This is cervical position, not whether the fetus is OA/OP.

What happens if a patient's Bishop score is low?

If the cervix is unfavorable, the patient may need cervical ripening before induction.

Cervical ripening agents such as prostaglandins and mechanical methods such as a balloon catheter, followed by induction methods such as oxytocin when appropriate.

Low Bishop

→ cervix isn't ready

→ ripen cervix

→ then induce labor when appropriate.

What is required to use vacuum/forceps?

Vacuum/forceps require full dilation, ruptured membranes, and an engaged head.

What is the danger of too much oxytocin?

Oxytocin makes the uterus contract. Too much oxytocin → too many contractions → placenta doesn't get enough recovery time → fetal oxygenation can decrease.

Oxytocin (Pitocin) stimulates uterine smooth muscle to produce contractions. It can be used to induce labor (start labor) or augment labor (strengthen labor that has already started).

The goal is not simply “more contractions.”

The goal is:

Effective contractions that produce cervical change while the fetus continues to tolerate labor

Why is oxytocin titrated?

Oxytocin is titrated—the dose is gradually adjusted according to uterine activity, labor progression, and fetal response.

The goal is:

Effective contractions that produce cervical change while the fetus continues to tolerate labor.

2. Why can too many contractions hurt the fetus?

During a contraction, the uterine muscle squeezes the blood vessels supplying the placenta.

That means uteroplacental blood flow temporarily decreases during a contraction.

Between contractions:

Uterus relaxes → blood flow improves → placenta is reperfused → fetus gets an opportunity to reoxygenate.

CONTRACTION → less placental blood flow

RELAXATION → placenta gets blood/oxygen again

So the fetus needs those rest periods between contractions.

What exactly is uterine tachysystole?

More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over a 30-minute window.

Notice it says:

MORE THAN 5 - Not “5 or more.”

5 contractions/10 min → not tachysystole by this definition

6 contractions/10 min → tachysystoleAnd it's assessed over time, not from one isolated 10-minute period.

“More than FIVE in TEN = too many.”

Patient receiving oxytocin has 6 contractions in 10 minutes and recurrent late decelerations. AFter stopping the oxytocin, what nursing interventions should be taken next?

Intrauterine resuscitation -"SION"

SIDE-LYING position - Reposition Mom laterally to improve maternal venous return and uteroplacental blood flow.

IV FLUID bolus - Improves maternal circulating volume and can support uteroplacental perfusion,

OXYGEN

NOTIFY provider Especially if the fetal tracing does not improve.

What if there is tachysystole but the fetal heart rate is still reassuring?

Tachysystole itself still needs attention, because excessive uterine activity can progress to fetal compromise.

But the urgency becomes particularly clear when you see:

Tachysystole + abnormal FHR

  • tachysystole describes what the uterus is doing, while the FHR tells you how the baby is tolerating it. They are related, but they are not the same thing.
  • For example, imagine the monitor shows 6 contractions in 10 minutes. That meets the definition of tachysystole (>5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes). But suppose the fetal heart rate is still 140 bpm with moderate variability, accelerations, and no concerning decelerations. In that moment, the uterus is contracting too frequently, but the fetus is not yet showing evidence of compromise.
What are the red flags for uterine rupture?

Oxytocin increases uterine activity. Excessive stimulation can increase concern for serious complications, particularly in patients with certain uterine scars/risk factors.

  • Sudden severe abdominal pain, abnormal FHR/bradycardia, cessation/change in contractions, vaginal bleeding, maternal hemodynamic instability, or loss of fetal station.

A particularly concerning clue is:

Baby was at +1 station and suddenly moves back to −1.

EMERGENCY!!!

What is the overall considerations for oxytocin?

OXYTOCIN

↓

stimulates CONTRACTIONS

↓

too much can cause TACHYSYSTOLE (>5 contractions / 10 min averaged over 30 min)

↓

inadequate RELAXATION

↓

decreased UTEROPLACENTAL PERFUSION

↓

decreased fetal OXYGENATION

↓

abnormal FHR, especially LATE DECELERATIONS

↓

STOP OXYTOCIN + INTRAUTERINE RESUSCITATION

Putting it together 10

What are the six occiput (vertex) positions?

Right or Left aligns with mom's body (baby's backbone)

Anterior or Posterior: Baby's backbone towards mom's front (anterior) or back (spine- Posterior)

Transverse: They are halfway b/w anterior and posterior (facing mom's sides)

ROP, LOP, ROA, LOA, ROT, LOT - 6 options

Middle letter is the landmark on the presenting part: O = occiput, so the head is presenting.

Example- ROP: Baby's backbone is on the right side of mom, and facing mom's spine, and the baby's occiput (head) is presenting in the cervix

✅ Corrected: the middle letter is the landmark, not the presentation.

What is the most advantageous position for birth?

LOA/ROA - left or right occiput anterior - so baby's head is presenting, their back is to the front/anterior of the mom, and they are canted left or right.

A vaginal exam is documented as left occiput posterior. Translate the three letters and name the labor symptom they predict.

Left side of the pelvis, occiput, posterior. The fetal back is toward the mother's back. She feels intense sacral pain. Hands-and-knees and sacral counterpressure are the matching nursing measures. Descent is often slower because internal rotation has farther to go.

1. A vaginal exam reads: 7 cm/90%/-2, vertex, LOA. What does each part mean?

7 cm dilated; 90% effaced; presenting part 2 cm above ischial spines/not engaged; head-first well-flexed presentation; occiput points toward maternal left-anterior pelvis.

A fetus is longitudinal, cephalic, vertex, ROP. Which term tells you the baby is head-first?

Cephalic tells you head-first;

vertex specifies the well-flexed cephalic presentation. ROP tells the direction of the occiput.

A client is 8 cm and says, “I have to push.” Is she in second stage?

No. She is in transition. Second stage begins at 10 cm and 100% effacement.

What is the most useful one-sentence distinction between presentation and position?

Presentation tells WHAT part comes first through the cervix; position tells WHERE that presenting landmark points in the maternal pelvis.

Key terms to remember

LIE = direction.

PRESENTATION = first part.

ATTITUDE = flexion.

POSITION = landmark direction.

STATION = descent.

VERTEX = flexed head-first.

OCCIPUT = landmark for vertex.

LOA = left occiput anterior.

0 STATION = engaged.

NEGATIVE = above spines.

POSITIVE = below spines / closer to birth.

A client calls and reports contractions for 2 hours that have increased with activity and did not decrease with rest and hydration. She denies leaking fluid and noticed bloody mucus when wiping. Which manifestation is she experiencing?

True contractions. They intensify with activity, they do not stop with rest and hydration, and bloody mucus is show from cervical change. Braxton Hicks ease with rest. Rupture is excluded by the denial of leaking. Fetal descent is not established by a phone report.

Contractions every 8 minutes, lasting 30 to 40 seconds. Cervix 2 cm, 50 percent effaced, station negative two. Which stage and phase is this?

first stage, latent or early phase. Mild, short, infrequent contractions and a cervix at 2 cm and 50 percent match the latent description.

Active on this deck starts near 6 cm.

Transition starts near 8 cm.

Second stage needs 10 cm and 100 percent. Station negative two does not assign the stage.

Fluid is green and thick at artificial rupture. Fetal heart rate is 140 with moderate variability and accelerations. What does the color mean, and what does it not mean?

Green/brown fluid → think MECONIUM

Meconium can occur with fetal stress, but seeing green fluid does not automatically mean the fetus is currently in distress.

  • Can get into lungs = respiratory issues

M7Fetal Monitoring, Comfort & Analgesia in Labor 40 cards

Fetal heart rate patterns 21

What is normal FHR and variability?

Normal baseline FHR = 110-160 bpm.

Moderate variability = 6-25 bpm and is reassuring. Variability reflects fetal autonomic nervous system function and oxygenation.

What does it mean when the FHR decelerates?

A deceleration simply means the fetal heart rate temporarily decreases below its baseline.

For example: Baseline FHR = 140

During a contraction, it falls to 110, then returns to 140.

That's a deceleration.

But a deceleration isn't automatically bad. The shape and timing tell you the likely cause.

What are the four patterns of FHR movement?

Variable deceleration - Cord compression - ⚠️ can be an issue

Early deceleration - Head compression - usually expected

Acceleration - baby doing well- reassuring

Late Deceleration - placental problem - concerning

What is the VEAL CHOP trick for understanding FHR?

Variable → Cord compression

Early → Head compression

Acceleration → OK

Late → Placental insufficiency

When a laboring client is having an issue with late deceleration, what steps should be taken (LION)?

L- Left side positioning

I- IV Fluid bolus

O - Oxygen

N- Notify/No Oxytocin/Pitocin

What is happening with early deceleration of the FHR?

EARLY deceleration = HEAD compression

What's happening? As the baby's head moves farther into the birth canal, a contraction puts pressure on the fetal head.

  • That pressure produces a temporary, gradual slowing of the fetal heart rate.
  • The important part is that the heart rate goes down at the same time as the contraction.

Think: Contraction squeezes head → heart rate slows → contraction releases → heart rate returns.

The FHR tracing therefore looks almost like a mirror image of the contraction.

What is happening with late deceleration of the FHR?

LATE deceleration = PLACENTAL insufficiency

What's happening? During a uterine contraction, blood flow through the placenta temporarily decreases.

Normally, the fetus tolerates this.

But if the placenta isn't delivering adequate oxygen, the fetus doesn't tolerate the contraction well.

The fetal heart rate then drops after the contraction has already started.

That's why it's called LATE.

Contraction → placenta can't provide enough oxygen → fetus responds afterward → FHR drops late.

So instead of matching the contraction, the FHR decrease is shifted to the right:

What are the nursing interventions for late deceleration?

If oxytocin (Pitocin) is running: STOP oxytocin.

Why? Oxytocin causes contractions. You don't want to keep stimulating contractions when the fetus isn't tolerating them.

Then:

Reposition Mom → generally lateral/side-lying.

IV fluid bolus → improve maternal circulating volume/perfusion.

Oxygen → follow your course/ATI protocol.

Notify provider.

If the pattern doesn't resolve, prepare for possible expedited delivery.

LATE = PLACENTA = BAD.

Or:

The contraction happened, and baby responded LATE.

What is occurring during variable deceleration of the FHR?

VARIABLE deceleration = CORD compression

Variable decelerations look very different.

Unlike early and late decelerations, they don't have a predictable relationship to the contraction.

They can happen: before, during, or after a contraction.

That's why they're called VARIABLE.

What's happening?

Something is compressing the umbilical cord

  • The cord carries blood between the fetus and placenta. If it's suddenly squeezed, fetal circulation is disrupted and the fetal heart rate can drop abruptly.
What are the key nursing interventions when a patient is experiencing variable deceleration?

Reposition Mom first.

Why?

You're trying to take pressure off the umbilical cord.

That's why the intervention actually matches the cause:

Cord compressed → MOVE MOM → hopefully relieve compression.

What can be done if repositioning the patient doesn't stop the variable deceleration?

Amnioinfusion for persistent variables.

Why would amnioinfusion help?

This makes much more sense if the membranes have ruptured.

Once amniotic fluid is lost, there may be less fluid cushioning the umbilical cord.

The cord can become compressed between:

baby ↔ uterine wall

Adding sterile fluid back into the uterus through an intrauterine catheter can provide additional cushion around the cord.

Variable → cord compression → reposition → persistent cases may need amnioinfusion.

A patient's water has broken; however the baby's head is not engaged and the FHR is below baseline for an extended period. What could be the issue?

CORD PROLAPSE

Membranes rupture

Baby's head is still high (negative station/not engaged)

Suddenly FHR drops dramatically and stays down

🚨 Think umbilical cord prolapse.

That's an obstetric emergency.

“After ROM + high station + prolonged drop → assess for prolapse.”

This is why you check the FHR after ROM

Why is acceleration of the FHR a good sign?

The fetal heart rate temporarily increases above baseline.

For example: Baseline = 140

Baby moves → heart rate increases to 160 → then returns to 140.

A fetus with an adequately oxygenated, functioning nervous system should be capable of responding.

So an acceleration is generally a:

“Hey, I'm doing fine in here!” signal.

That's why VEAL CHOP says:

A → O

Acceleration → OK

No treatment.

Easy way to remember FHR movement?

EARLY mirrors the contraction.

LATE is shifted to the right of the contraction.

VARIABLE is abrupt and does not have a consistent relationship to contractions.

What are the three categories of FHR?

Category I: normal/reassuring — baseline 110–160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations; early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absent.

Category II: indeterminate — anything not Category I or III; requires continued surveillance and correction of reversible causes.

Category III: abnormal — absent variability PLUS recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia; or sinusoidal pattern. Resuscitate while preparing for prompt delivery if unresolved.

FHR deceleration begins with the contraction, reaches its lowest point at the contraction peak, and returns to baseline by the end. Pattern and cause?

Answer: Early deceleration caused by fetal head compression.

FHR deceleration begins after the contraction starts and returns after the contraction ends. Pattern and cause?

Answer: Late deceleration caused by uteroplacental insufficiency.

VEAL CHOP MINE

FHR Pattern: VEAL Cause; CHOP Intervention: MINE

Variable deceleration, Cord Compression, Move mom

Early deceleration, Head compression, Intervention not needed

Accelerations, OK, No intervention

Late deceleration, Placental insufficiency, Emergency: act now (stop oxytocin, side-lying, IV fluid, oxygen, notify)

The fetal heart tracing shows abrupt drops that do not line up with contractions, with a rapid return to baseline. What is the cause, and what is the first move?

Variable deceleration = cord compression

Move the mother. Abrupt shape and variable timing are the variable-deceleration picture. Priority is maternal repositioning, often left lateral or hands-and-knees. Oxygen and amnioinfusion are later steps if position change fails.

Early decelerations mirror each contraction in a client who is 8 cm. What is the priority?

Continue monitoring. No intervention is required for the pattern itself. Early decelerations are head compression and mirror the contraction. They are an expected finding as the head descends in active labor and transition. A vaginal exam to confirm progress is reasonable. Intrauterine resuscitation is not.

What are the four types of FHR variability?

Absent: amplitude undetectable

Minimal: 5 bpm or less

Moderate: 6 to 25 bpm (reassuring)

Marked: more than 25 bpm

Pain relief and anesthesia 19

What are the nursing interventions and concerns related to epidurals?
  • Watch for maternal hypotension → decreased placental perfusion → late decelerations.

Monitor BP and FHR; maintain lateral positioning and fluids as ordered.

When is a pudendal block used?

perineal anesthesia in second stage / repair.

When is spinal anesthesia used?

Spinal: commonly used for cesarean birth; post-dural puncture headache is worse upright.

What are common non-pharm interventions for labor pains?

Massage:

  • counter pressure (counteracts contraction pressure)

Positioning: walk, rock, birth ball, freq movement

Patterned breathing

Music, aroma, oils, guided imagery

Biofeedback

Hypnosis/hypnobirthing

Pain is subjective- listen to client.

Use OLDCARTS or CALDERRA to assess pain.

How can heat and cold be used for nonpharmacologic pain relief?

Ice packs

Cool washcloth

Warm Packs

Heating pad (but not too hot- be careful)

Warm bath/shower

Hydrotherapy

What are some more invasive non-pharm pain interventions?

Acupuncture

Acupressure

TENS

Intradermal injection of sterile water

  • Stimulates the release of endorphins to reduce pain sensation
What is the difference b/w analgesia vs anesthesia?

Analgesia: Reduces sensation of pain for limited period of time

Anesthesia: Reduces all sensation of pain for a set length of time.

  • Narcotics
  • Regional: Epidural, spinal (breast, down)
  • Local: infiltration, pudendal
  • General: benefits/risks - More risks!
What is a pudendal block?

Local anesthetic (lidocaine) just before birth for perineal numbing; injected thru vagina.

Numbs the perineum and lower vagina. It does not relieve contraction pain, because it does not reach the cervix or uterus.

  • Used if there's scarring, episiotomy, big baby, and may be some tearing
  • Useful for repair post-delivery

✅ Corrected: the set said it numbs "from the cervix down".

How is a lumbar epidural block administered?

Injected at L3-L4 for first stage of labor with a continuous block, lasts through birth.

  • Onset within minutes, and the continuous infusion keeps it going; loss of pain perception for labor contractions and birth
  • could cause maternal HypoT
  • Can slow labor if given too early; pushing feeling is stopped which can prolong 2nd stage
  • May have an impact on fetus after birth.
Difference b/w epidural and spinal?
  • Spinal goes into the subarachnoid space where CSF is. One time administration lasts up to 4 hours.
  • Can cause a spinal headache due to CSF leakage.
  • Epidural is a continuous infusion through a catheter in the epidural space.

always bolus +500ml IV before procedure is done to help with rapid hypotension. Helps circulatory system and helps to rehydrate.

Why is general anesthesia used?

Emergency situation and the baby needs to be taken out ASAP.

Prepare equipment: Laryngoscope, endotracheal tube, breathing bag with 100% O2, suction cath.

How is anoxia related to contraction pain?

Blood vessels constrict during contractions, reducing oxygen to uterine and cervical muscle fibers; the resulting ischemia activates nociceptors (similar to angina).

How are systemic opioids used in labor?

Fentanyl, nalbuphine, butorphanol; cross placenta and can cause neonatal respiratory depression if given close to birth.

Naloxone (Narcan) | Opioid antagonist used for maternal or neonatal respiratory depression; avoid in opioid-dependent patients because of withdrawal risk.

What is a blood patch and when is it used?

10-20 mL of autologous blood injected into the epidural space to seal a cerebrospinal fluid leak and treat post-dural puncture headache.

Post-dural puncture headache | Severe positional headache (worse upright) from cerebrospinal fluid leakage after dural puncture; treated with fluids, lie flat, analgesics, and blood patch if severe.

What is a major risk with general anesthesia?

General anesthesia risks - Used for emergencies or when regional is contraindicated;

Major risks = maternal aspiration (Mendelson syndrome) and hypoxia; patient is asleep.

Sodium citrate | Non-particulate antacid given before general anesthesia to raise gastric pH and reduce damage if aspiration occurs.

Why is a patient preloaded with IV bolus fluids before an epidural?

Intravenous crystalloid bolus (commonly 500–1000 mL) given to reduce the risk of hypotension from sympathetic blockade.

Hypotension after regional block = Priority: fluid bolus, lateral position, oxygen if needed, notify provider; can cause late decelerations from reduced uteroplacental perfusion.

What are the contraindications to regional anesthesia?

Coagulopathy, infection at insertion site, severe hypovolemia, patient refusal, certain neurologic conditions; thrombocytopenia is a common example.

What is a motor block after an epidural?

Expected with higher concentrations of local anesthetic; Nursing intervention: protect lower extremities from injury and assist with first ambulation until sensation and strength return.

Also- Pruritus after epidural | Common side effect of epidural opioids; usually treated with small doses of naloxone, antihistamines, or other agents per protocol.

What opioid analgesics are used in labor?

Analgesics = do not eliminate pain completely but do reduce the sensation of pain for a limited period of time.

Butorphanol tartrate (Stadol)

Nalbuphine (Nubain)

Morphine Sulfate,

Fentanyl (Sublimaze)

Narcotic analgesics – may be given during labor because of their potent effect, but all drugs in this category cause maternal respiratory depression as well as fetal CNS and respiratory depression, so should not be given within one hour of delivery.
